messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Phong was seventy when he volunteered as a data analyst for a humanitarian organization in a contested region of the Middle East. What began as a desk job ended abruptly when his convoy was ambushed on a supply run. He spent six hours pinned in a collapsed clinic with two wounded colleagues, listening to gunfire and the shouts of armed men who ransacked the supplies. One of the men, a young fighter, laughed as he kicked a dying medic. Phong could not move, could not help, could only press himself against the cold floor and wait. That moment—the laughter, the helplessness, the stench of blood and diesel—never left him. In the months after returning home, the memory did not fade. It intruded without warning: the feel of the concrete against his cheek, the crack of a rifle, the medic’s shallow breaths. When the memory surfaced, it felt as though he were still in that clinic—not remembering, but reliving. Because the memory came back so vividly, he began to see threads of it everywhere — in the way a stranger laughed, in the smell of diesel at a gas station, in the quality of afternoon light — so that once-innocent moments now felt charged with danger. The scene would play over and over, a film he could not stop. At first he tried to push it away, but the images kept coming, especially at night. He began waking from nightmares with his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, the dream residue clinging to him like smoke. Those mornings were the worst: he would lie still, certain that if he opened his eyes he would see the ceiling of the clinic, not his bedroom. The waking moments after a nightmare were powerful triggers. They brought the memory roaring back, and they also fed his darkest fear: that his mind was unraveling. He began to believe that his reactions meant he was going crazy. He also grew terrified of his own anger. Once, while waiting in line at the grocery store, a customer cursed at the cashier—a small thing, but Phong felt a surge of rage so sudden and intense that he feared he might lash out physically. He retreated, shaking, convinced that he could lose control and do something terrible. The world, he concluded, was a dangerous place, and he was a danger too. To manage these fears, Phong adopted a series of careful strategies. He avoided news reports of any conflict, turning off the television the moment a war zone appeared. He rehearsed conversations before every interaction, running through possible questions and his responses, because he was terrified that an unexpected comment might trigger his rage or reveal his instability. In public, he constantly scanned his environment, checking doorways, scanning faces for signs of threat. This hypervigilance kept his body on constant alert—shoulders tight, jaw clenched, ready to react to nothing. Yet the very acts of rehearsing and scanning kept the memory alive. When he rehearsed a conversation, his mind would drift back to the clinic, as if the mental vigilance itself summoned the images. The checking behavior also increased his sense of being trapped: every scan of a room reminded him that he was always on guard, always without options. He came to see his own strategies as part of the threat—they confirmed that the world was unsafe and that he was barely holding on. Once he had decided the world was dangerous, ordinary sounds became potential threats — a car backfiring, a raised voice in the next aisle — and each one pulled him back into the clinic. He noticed that his irritability had grown. A neighbor’s loud music, a delay in a software update—small frustrations triggered angry outbursts that frightened him. He would then avoid human contact, canceling plans with his adult children, telling himself he needed to protect them from his temper. His job as a data scientist, once a source of pride, became grueling: data sets required intense focus, but he could not concentrate. He spent hours rerunning the same analysis, because every time he tried to work, the memory of the clinic would surface, and he would lose his train of thought. The cycle tightened. A news headline (trigger) would spark the memory, which reinforced his appraisal that the world was dangerous, which led him to scan his surroundings (maladaptive strategy), which in turn made him feel trapped, which made him think of the clinic again. Each component fed the next, and he became a prisoner of his own vigilance. Now, at eighty, Phong has been retired for two years, but the symptoms have not lessened. He reaches for the remote every time a news broadcast begins. He rehearses the simplest phone calls. His children have stopped visiting as frequently, unsure how to reach him. What finally brought him to therapy was a morning when he woke from a nightmare and could not, for several seconds, remember where he was. He had come to believe that he was losing his mind, and he was terrified of the anger he felt toward a stranger who had cut him off in traffic. He hopes that naming the fear might loosen its grip, but he is not certain that talking about the clinic will help—or that he can bear to revisit it. Each avoidance deepened the trigger — the very act of turning off the TV made the image more vivid, so that the next time he saw even a news headline, the memory was already waiting.
